title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXVIII
paragraphs:
“C’est beaucoup que le jugement des hommes sur les actions humaines;
tôt ou tard il devient efficace.”—GUIZOT.

Sir James Chettam found nothing to approve of in Mr. Brooke’s new activities, but disapproval was easier than prevention. One day, arriving alone to have lunch with the Cadwalladers, Sir James explained why he had come without his wife—
“I can’t speak to you freely with Celia there: it might hurt her feelings. Really, it wouldn’t be right.”

“I know what you mean—the ‘Pioneer’ at the Grange!” Mrs. Cadwallader broke in before her friend had quite finished. “It’s dreadful, this new habit of buying whistles and blowing them where everyone can hear. Staying in bed all day playing dominoes, like poor Lord Plessy, would at least be private, and easier to bear.”

“I see the ‘Trumpet’ has started attacking our friend Brooke,” said the Rector, leaning back with the same comfortable smile he would have worn if the attacks had been directed at himself. “Some tremendous sarcasm about a landlord within easy reach of Middlemarch who collects his own rents and gives nothing back.”
“I do wish Brooke would stop doing that,” Sir James said, his brow contracting in a small, irritated frown.

“But is he actually going to stand for election?” asked Mr. Cadwallader. “I saw Farebrother yesterday. He leans towards the Whigs himself, waves the flag for Brougham and Useful Knowledge; that’s the worst I can say of him. He tells me Brooke is building up quite a following. His chief supporter is Bulstrode the banker. Still, Farebrother thinks Brooke would fare badly at the nomination.”

“Exactly,” Sir James said earnestly. “I’ve been making inquiries. I never knew anything about Middlemarch politics before: the county has always been my concern. Brooke is relying on their throwing Oliver out because he supports Peel. But Hawley tells me that if they put forward a Whig, it’s bound to be Bagster—one of those candidates from heaven knows where, but firmly against the Ministers and an experienced man in Parliament. Hawley is rather rough; he forgot whom he was talking to. He said that if Brooke wanted people to throw things at him, there were cheaper ways than taking to the election platform.”
“I warned you all,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, spreading her hands. “Long ago I told Humphrey that Mr. Brooke was heading for a splash in the mud. And now he’s made it.”
“Well, he might have decided to marry,” the Rector observed. “That would have landed him in a more serious mess than a little flirtation with politics.”
“He may do that next,” Mrs. Cadwallader replied, “once he’s emerged from the mud with a fever.”

“It’s his own dignity that concerns me most,” said Sir James. “Naturally the family connection makes me care all the more. But he’s getting older, and I hate to think of him exposing himself like this. They’ll dig up everything they can against him.”
“I suppose persuasion would be useless,” said the Rector. “Brooke combines stubbornness and changeability in such a peculiar way. Have you tried talking to him about it?”

“Well, no,” Sir James admitted. “I’m reluctant to seem to be giving orders. But I’ve talked to young Ladislaw, whom Brooke is turning into his general assistant. Ladislaw seems clever enough to do anything. I thought I should hear his views, and he’s against Brooke standing this time. I think he’ll bring him round; I think we may put off the nomination.”
“I understand,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, nodding. “The independent candidate hasn’t learned his speeches properly yet.”

“But Ladislaw—there’s another tiresome business,” Sir James continued. “We’ve had him to dinner at the Hall two or three times—you’ve met him, by the way—as Brooke’s guest and Casaubon’s relation, thinking he was only paying a short visit. Now I find all Middlemarch talking about him as the editor of the ‘Pioneer.’ Stories are circulating about a foreign scribbler, an emissary from abroad, and all the rest.”
“Casaubon won’t care for that,” said the Rector.
“Ladislaw does have some foreign ancestry,” Sir James replied. “I hope he doesn’t take up extreme views and drag Brooke along with him.”

“Oh, that Mr. Ladislaw is a dangerous young fellow,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, “with his opera songs and his quick tongue. A kind of Byronic hero—a romantic conspirator, I should say. And Thomas Aquinas isn’t fond of him. I could see that when the picture was brought over.”

“I’m reluctant to raise the subject with Casaubon,” said Sir James. “He has more right to intervene than I do. But the whole affair is disagreeable. What a role for anyone with respectable connections to put himself in! One of those newspaper men! Just look at Keck, who runs the ‘Trumpet.’ I saw him with Hawley the other day. His articles are sound enough, I believe, but he’s such a vulgar fellow that I wished he supported the other side.”

“What else can you expect from these petty Middlemarch newspapers?” asked the Rector. “I doubt you could find a man of much standing anywhere to promote interests he doesn’t really care about, for wages that scarcely keep his elbows covered.”
“Exactly. That’s why it’s so irritating that Brooke should place a man with a connection of sorts to the family in such a position. Personally, I think Ladislaw rather foolish to accept it.”
“It’s Aquinas’s fault,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “Why didn’t he use his connections to get Ladislaw an attaché’s post, or send him to India? That’s how families dispose of troublesome young branches.”
“There’s no telling how far the trouble may spread,” Sir James said anxiously. “But if Casaubon says nothing, what am I to do?”

“My dear Sir James,” said the Rector, “let’s not make too much of it. Very likely the whole thing will amount to nothing. In a month or two Brooke and young Master Ladislaw will tire of each other. Ladislaw will fly away, Brooke will sell the ‘Pioneer,’ and everything will return to normal.”

“We have one good hope: he won’t enjoy feeling his money trickle away,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “If I had an itemized list of election costs, I could frighten him. Grand words like Expenditure are no use. I wouldn’t lecture him on bloodletting; I’d empty a pot of leeches over him. What we good, stingy people dislike is having our sixpences sucked out of us.”

“And he won’t enjoy having his faults dragged into the open,” said Sir James. “There’s his management of the estate. They’ve already started on that. It really pains me to see it; the trouble is right under our noses. I do think a man has a duty to do his best for his land and tenants, particularly in such hard times.”

“Perhaps the ‘Trumpet’ will stir him into changing things, and some good will come of the affair,” said the Rector. “I’d certainly welcome it. There would be less grumbling when my tithe was paid. I don’t know how I’d manage if Tipton didn’t have a fixed payment in place of the tithe.”

“I want him to employ a competent man to look after the place. I want him to take Garth back,” said Sir James. “He dismissed Garth twelve years ago, and things have gone downhill ever since. I’m considering having Garth manage my own estate: he’s drawn up such an excellent plan for my buildings, and Lovegood isn’t quite equal to the work. But Garth wouldn’t take on Tipton again unless Brooke gave him complete control.”

“And quite right too,” said the Rector. “Garth is an independent man, original and straightforward. Once, while doing a valuation for me, he told me plainly that clergymen rarely understood business and did harm when they interfered. Yet he said it as calmly and respectfully as though he were discussing sailors. He’d transform the parish of Tipton if Brooke let him manage it. I wish you could bring that about with help from the ‘Trumpet.’”

“If Dorothea had stayed close to her uncle, there might have been a chance,” said Sir James. “In time she might have gained some influence over him, and she was always troubled about the estate. She had remarkably good ideas on such matters. Now Casaubon occupies her completely. Celia complains about it a good deal. Since his attack, we can scarcely persuade her to dine with us.” Sir James finished with a look combining pity and disgust. Mrs. Cadwallader shrugged, as if to say that she, at least, was unlikely to find anything surprising in that quarter.
“Poor Casaubon!” said the Rector. “It was a nasty attack. He looked broken when I saw him at the Archdeacon’s the other day.”
“The fact is,” Sir James resumed, choosing not to dwell on these attacks, “Brooke wishes his tenants no harm, or anyone else. But he’s fallen into this habit of shaving a little off every expense.”
“Well, that’s a blessing,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “It helps him recognize himself in the morning. He may not know his own opinions, but he knows his own pocket.”
“I don’t believe a man saves money by being stingy with his land,” said Sir James.

“Oh, stinginess can be abused like any other virtue. Keeping your own pigs thin won’t do,” said Mrs. Cadwallader, who had stood up to look through the window. “But speak of an independent politician, and here he comes.”
“What! Brooke?” her husband asked.
“Yes. Now, Humphrey, you work on him with the ‘Trumpet,’ and I’ll apply the leeches. What will you do, Sir James?”

“The truth is, with our relationship, I dislike being the one to bring it up with Brooke. It’s all so unpleasant. I do wish people would conduct themselves like gentlemen,” said the good baronet, feeling that this was a simple and comprehensive scheme for society’s welfare.

“So here you all are, eh?” said Mr. Brooke, shuffling from one to the other and shaking hands. “I meant to go up to the Hall later, Chettam. Pleasant to find everyone together, though, you know. Well, what do you make of things? Moving rather fast! Lafitte was right when he said, ‘Since yesterday, a century has passed away.’ Across the water they’re already in the next century, you know. Moving faster than we are.”
“Indeed they are,” said the Rector, picking up the newspaper. “The ‘Trumpet’ accuses you of falling behind. Have you seen it?”
“Eh? No,” said Mr. Brooke. He dropped his gloves into his hat and hurriedly adjusted his eyeglass. But Mr. Cadwallader held on to the paper, and said with amusement in his eyes—

“Look at this! It’s all about a landlord not far from Middlemarch who collects his own rents. They call him the most backward-looking man in the county—‘retrogressive.’ I think they must have learned that word from your ‘Pioneer.’”

“Oh, that’s Keck—an ignorant fellow, you know. Retrogressive, indeed! Excellent. He thinks it means destructive. They want to paint me as a destroyer, you know,” said Mr. Brooke, buoyed by the cheerfulness an opponent’s supposed ignorance usually supplies.

“I think he understands the word. Here are a few sharp jabs. _If asked to describe a man who is retrogressive in the worst sense, we would name someone who calls himself a reformer of our constitution while allowing everything directly under his charge to decay: a philanthropist who cannot bear to see one scoundrel hanged, yet lets five honest tenants half starve; a man who screams about corruption while charging crushing rents; who bellows himself red over rotten boroughs, yet accepts a rotten gate in every field on his farms. No doubt he is wonderfully generous towards Leeds and Manchester: he would give them any number of representatives, provided those gentlemen paid for their seats themselves. What he objects to giving is a little rent money back to help a tenant buy livestock, or money for repairs to keep the weather out of a tenant’s barn, or to make his home look less like an Irish peasant’s hut. But we all know the joker’s definition of a philanthropist: a man whose charity grows in proportion to the square of the distance._ And so it continues. The rest explains what kind of lawmaker such a philanthropist would be,” the Rector concluded. He dropped the paper, clasped his hands behind his head, and regarded Mr. Brooke with amused impartiality.

“Well, that’s rather good, you know,” said Mr. Brooke, picking up the paper. He tried to take the attack as lightly as his neighbour, but his colour rose and his smile was nervous. “That bit about bellowing himself red over rotten boroughs—I’ve never made a speech about rotten boroughs in my life. And all this bellowing myself red—these men don’t understand good satire. Satire ought to be true up to a point, you know. I remember reading that somewhere in ‘The Edinburgh.’ It must be true up to a point.”

“But the remark about the gates does hit home,” said Sir James, anxious to proceed delicately. “Dagley told me the other day he hadn’t a decent gate anywhere on his farm. Garth has designed a new kind. I wish you’d try it. A man ought to put some of his timber to that use.”
“You like fancy farming, Chettam, you know,” said Mr. Brooke, apparently scanning the ‘Trumpet’s’ columns. “That’s your hobby, and you don’t object to paying for it.”

“I thought standing for Parliament was the most expensive hobby in existence,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “They said the last man who failed at Middlemarch—wasn’t he called Giles?—spent ten thousand pounds and lost because he hadn’t spent enough on bribes. What a bitter thought to live with!”
“Someone was saying,” the Rector added with a laugh, “that for bribery East Retford couldn’t begin to compare with Middlemarch.”

“Nothing of the sort,” said Mr. Brooke. “It’s the Tories who bribe, you know. Hawley and his people buy men drinks—hot codlings and that sort of thing—and take voters to the poll drunk. But they won’t have everything their own way from now on—not in future, you know. I admit Middlemarch is a little backward; the freemen are a little backward. But we’ll educate them, bring them forward, you know. The best people there support us.”
“Hawley says some of your supporters will hurt your chances,” Sir James remarked. “He says Bulstrode the banker will do you harm.”

“And if they throw things at you,” Mrs. Cadwallader put in, “half the rotten eggs will express their hatred of your committee member. Good heavens! Imagine being pelted for holding the wrong opinions. And wasn’t there a story about a man they pretended to carry triumphantly in a chair, only to drop him deliberately into a rubbish heap!”

“Being pelted is nothing beside having your faults exposed,” said the Rector. “That’s what I’d fear if we parsons had to win advancement on an election platform. I’d dread their adding up all my days spent fishing. Honestly, I believe truth is the hardest thing anyone can throw at you.”
“The point is,” said Sir James, “a man who enters public life must expect the consequences. He must put himself beyond the reach of slander.”

“My dear Chettam, that sounds very fine, you know,” Mr. Brooke replied. “But how do you protect yourself against slander? Read history—consider ostracism, persecution, martyrdom, and so forth. They always happen to the best men. But what’s that line in Horace? _Fiat justitia, ruat_ … something or other.”
“Exactly,” said Sir James, rather more heatedly than usual. “By being safe from slander I mean being able to point to the facts and disprove it.”
“And paying the bills you have chosen to run up yourself hardly makes you a martyr,” Mrs. Cadwallader added.

It was Sir James’s obvious irritation, however, that affected Mr. Brooke most. “Well, Chettam, you know,” he said, rising, taking his hat and leaning on his stick, “you and I follow different systems. With your farms you believe in spending freely. I don’t claim my own system works in every circumstance—in every circumstance, you understand.”
“Rents ought to be reassessed from time to time,” said Sir James. “An occasional rebate is all very well, but I prefer a fair valuation. What do you think, Cadwallader?”

“I agree. In Brooke’s place I’d silence the ‘Trumpet’ immediately: get Garth to revalue the farms and give him a free hand over gates and repairs. That’s my assessment of the political situation,” said the Rector. He hooked his thumbs into his armholes, making himself look broader, and laughed towards Mr. Brooke.

“That would look very grand, you know,” said Mr. Brooke. “But name another landlord who has seized his tenants’ property for unpaid rent as rarely as I have. I keep the old tenants on. I’m extraordinarily easy with them, I assure you, extraordinarily easy. I have my own ideas and stand by them. A man who does that always gets called eccentric, inconsistent, and so on. When I alter my course, it will be according to my own ideas.”
At that point Mr. Brooke remembered a parcel he had forgotten to send from the Grange, and hurriedly said goodbye to everyone.

“I didn’t mean to presume with Brooke,” said Sir James. “I can see he’s irritated. But whatever he says about keeping old tenants, the truth is that no new tenant would take those farms on the present terms.”

“I fancy he’ll come round eventually,” said the Rector. “But Elinor, you were pulling against us. You wanted to frighten him out of spending, while we wanted to frighten him into it. Better let him try to win popularity and discover that his reputation as a landlord blocks the way. I don’t think the ‘Pioneer,’ or Ladislaw, or Brooke making speeches to Middlemarch matters two straws. What matters is whether the people of Tipton parish can live comfortably.”

“Excuse me, but you two took the wrong approach,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “You should have shown him how bad management costs him money; then we’d all have been pulling together. If you mount him on the horse of politics, I warn you what may happen. Riding sticks at home and calling them ideas was harmless enough.”
